The short mackerel, Rastrelliger brachysoma, exhibits a life history typical of fast-growing tropical scombrids, with rapid early development setting the stage for its relatively compressed adult phase. Field surveys conducted in the Gulf of Thailand indicate that the yolk-sac larval stage is remarkably brief; during the monsoon season at a stable water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], the interval between fertilization and eclosion is approximately 2.7 days [ab = approximately 2.7 days]. Newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The dry weight at birth is approximately 0.00045 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00045 grams]. This accelerated embryonic period is an adaptation to warm, productive waters where high predation pressure on early life stages favors a rapid transition to a free-swimming, feeding larval phase. The efficiency of this early development is further reflected in the modest dry weight of the hatchling, which has been estimated from studies on congeneric species with similar egg dimensions.

Sexual maturation in Rastrelliger brachysoma occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to its ultimate dimensions, a pattern consistent with many small, fast-growing clupeoids and scombrids. Detailed sampling of the commercial catch along the western coast of Sumatra revealed that individuals typically reach puberty at a total length of 17.3 cm [Lp = 17.3 cm]. This length marks the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the beginning of vitellogenesis in females, although full reproductive capability may lag slightly behind this initial maturational milestone. The attainment of this length is generally achieved within the first year of life, given the abundant food resources available in tropical pelagic ecosystems. The moderate size at first maturity allows the species to begin contributing to the spawning stock early, a critical factor in maintaining population stability under moderate fishing pressure, and it stands in contrast to larger, longer-lived scombrids that defer reproduction for several years.

The maximum total length recorded for Rastrelliger brachysoma from extensive fishery-independent surveys in the South China Sea is 34.5 cm [Li = 34.5 cm], a value that represents the asymptotic size approached by the oldest and largest individuals in the population. Corresponding to this ultimate length, the ultimate wet weight of an adult fish has been estimated using a length-weight relationship derived from composite data across its geographic range, yielding a value of 485 grams [Wwi = 485 grams] for a specimen at the asymptotic length. This body mass represents the maximum somatic investment an individual attains, after which growth slows considerably and energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward reproductive output rather than further increases in structural size. The length-weight relationship reveals a slightly positive allometric growth pattern, indicating that older fish become somewhat deeper-bodied relative to their length, a common feature among fishes that undergo a shift from a predominantly planktivorous to a more varied diet as they mature.

Reproductive effort in this species is substantial and tightly linked to the warm, stable thermal regime of its tropical habitat. Under typical conditions, with surface waters remaining near 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C] throughout much of the spawning season, females produce a large number of small, pelagic eggs. Spawning occurs in multiple batches over an extended season, and the combined output translates to an average daily reproductive rate of approximately 101 eggs per female per day. Each individual spawning event is characterized by the release of several thousand oocytes, and females spawn repeatedly at short intervals. This high fecundity is a common strategy among small pelagic fish, compensating for high rates of egg and larval mortality in the plankton. The energetic demands of such sustained gamete production are met by continuous feeding on zooplankton, and the warm water temperatures facilitate rapid ovarian recrudescence between successive spawning bouts, ensuring a steady supply of ripe oocytes.

The overall lifespan of Rastrelliger brachysoma is comparatively short for a fish of its ultimate body size, a life-history trait aligned with its rapid growth and early maturity. Longevity estimates derived from otolith increment analysis indicate that the maximum lifespan in wild populations is approximately 2 years [am = approximately 2 years], with these age determinations made on fish sampled from waters at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. Very few individuals survive beyond this age, as natural mortality and fishing pressure combine to limit the adult population to a few annual cohorts. This compressed life cycle means that most reproductive output is concentrated within a single spawning season, and iteroparity, while present, typically involves only two or three spawning events per lifetime. The combination of early puberty, high fecundity, and a short lifespan defines Rastrelliger brachysoma as a classic r-selected species, well-adapted to the variable and productive pelagic environment of the Indo-West Pacific.
